Abstract
Precise water body segmentation in satellite imagery plays a vital role in environmental monitoring, water resource man-
agement, and disaster prevention. This study introduces a high-performance segmentation framework leveraging Sentinel-2 
imagery, integrating advanced methodologies to enhance data integrity and segmentation accuracy. To increase dataset 
diversity and model generalization, StyleGAN3-based augmentation was implemented, yielding a 5% accuracy improvement 
over conventional methods. An Attention-Guided Denoising Autoencoder with Skip Connection (AG-DAES) was utilized 
for noise reduction, effectively preserving spatial details and strengthening segmentation robustness. To address missing and 
corrupted pixels, Bi-ConvRNN was employed for pixel restoration, significantly boosting performance. Additionally, the 
Particle Swarm Dandelion Optimization (PSDO) algorithm was used for hyperparameter tuning, contributing to an additional 
3–5% accuracy gain. Feature extraction was refined through the Multiscale Strip Convolution Module (MSSCM), enhanc-
ing spatial-spectral representation and leading to a 6–8% accuracy increase. The segmentation process was executed using 
the Map U-Net model, which, after integrating all proposed improvements, achieved state-of-the-art accuracy exceeding 
99%. A comparative study demonstrated that the proposed framework outperforms existing methods, particularly in com-
plex scenarios involving vegetation interference, occlusions, and mixed land–water transitions. This adaptable and scalable 
approach sets a new standard for water body segmentation in satellite image analysis, offering a powerful tool for future 
research in the field.

Introduction
Satellite imagery plays a vital role in monitoring and 
managing water bodies, such as lakes, rivers, and oceans, 
which are essential components of our ecosystem. Accu-
rate segmentation of water bodies is critical for applications 
in environmental monitoring, disaster management, and 
resource planning (Dube et al. 2015). Sentinel-2 satellite 
imagery provides comprehensive and detailed observations 
of Earth’s surface, enabling the identification and analysis of 
water bodies across large spatial and temporal scales. Tasks 
such as detecting changes in water extent, monitoring sea-
sonal variations, and assessing flood risks heavily depend 
on precise and efficient segmentation techniques. However, 
achieving high-precision segmentation remains challenging 
due to the complexity of satellite data and environmental 
variability (Gong, et al. 2024).
Deep learning has significantly improved water body seg-
mentation in satellite imagery by automating feature extrac-
tion and enhancing accuracy (Yuan, et al. 2021). However, 
existing deep learning-based methods still face critical 
challenges, including sensitivity to noise (Rahaman, et al. 
2022), incomplete pixel information (Sun, et al. 2024a), and 
spectral inconsistencies caused by environmental variations 
(Gautam and Singhai 2024). These limitations often result

Recent advancements in deep learning have further 
enhanced image segmentation capabilities, particularly 
through improvements in Convolutional Neural Networks 
(CNNs) and Vision Transformer (ViT)-based models. Since 
2023, CNN architectures such as ConvNeXt and Efficient-
NetV2 have optimized feature extraction efficiency while 
reducing computational complexity (Guo, et al. 2022). 
Additionally, hybrid CNN-Transformer models have dem-
onstrated enhanced generalization for complex image anal-
ysis tasks (Liu and Yang 2025). Simultaneously, Vision 
Transformers have evolved with architectures like Swin 
Transformer V2 and MaxViT, which improve spatial atten-
tion mechanisms, making them highly effective for large-
scale segmentation tasks (Chiabodo 2024). Furthermore, 
research has shown that incorporating quantitative regulari-
zation techniques and optimized data distribution learning 
significantly enhances ViT-based classification and object 
detection in remote sensing imagery (Gao, et al. 2024; Hu, 
et al. 2024a). These advancements collectively contribute to 
state-of-the-art performance in satellite image segmentation, 
offering new directions for improving water body delinea-
tion in remote sensing applications (Affek and Szymański 
2024).
Water body segmentation in satellite imagery presents 
several challenges due to spectral overlap, noise, and envi-
ronmental variations (Wieland, et al. 2023). Distinguishing 
water bodies from similar land features, such as wetlands, 
muddy terrains, and shaded regions, is particularly difficult 
(Nagaraj and Kumar 2024). Additionally, atmospheric effects 
like cloud cover and sun glare introduce further complexi-
ties, often leading to misclassification (Han, et al. 2024). 
To address these challenges, optimization of deep learning 
frameworks is essential. U-Net, a widely used model for 
segmentation, has demonstrated strong performance in many 
remote sensing applications (Li, et al. 2024a). However, its 
ability to accurately delineate water boundaries is limited 
by its reliance on local spatial features and its susceptibil-
ity to noise. Enhancing U-Net with attention mechanisms, 
multiscale feature extraction, and optimized hyperparam-
eters can significantly improve its robustness against these 
issues, leading to more precise water body delineation (Fan, 
et al. 2022).
Data augmentation is an essential step in deep learning to 
improve the diversity and size of training datasets, reducing 
overfitting and enhancing generalization. Techniques like 
GANs (Generative Adversarial Networks), CycleGANs, and 
StyleGANs have been employed for generating synthetic 
data that closely resembles real-world images (Bauer, et al. 
2024; Huang, et al. 2024). In this study, StyleGAN3 is uti-
lized for data augmentation, offering superior capabilities 
in capturing intricate spatial patterns and textures compared 
to traditional methods like flipping or rotation. Recent stud-
ies have also explored pure data correction techniques and 
ensemble-based augmentation strategies to further enhance 
classification accuracy in remote sensing images (Amitrano, 
et al. 2024; Hänsch 2024).
Noise reduction is a critical step in satellite image anal-
ysis to eliminate distortions caused by sensor limitations 
or environmental factors. Advanced deep learning-based 
methods, such as DnCNN (Denoising Convolutional Neural 
Network), Noise2 Noise, and Attention-Guided Denoising 
Autoencoders (AG-DAEs), have shown promising results in 
removing noise while preserving important details (Wang, 
et al. 2024a). This study employs an enhanced version, the 
Attention-Guided Denoising Autoencoder with Skip Con-
nections (AG-DAES), to focus on salient regions while 
maintaining fine-grained image fidelity, ensuring cleaner 
inputs for subsequent processing (Rahman, et al 2024).
Pixel imputation addresses the issue of missing or cor-
rupted data in satellite imagery, which can hinder accurate 
segmentation. Methods such as PixelCNN, RNN-Impute, 
and ConvRNNs have been successfully used for spatial and 
temporal imputation tasks (Zhang, et al. 2024a). This study 
adopts Bi-ConvRNN, a bidirectional convolutional recurrent 
network, to predict missing values by leveraging both spatial 
coherence and contextual dependencies, thereby ensuring 
accurate restoration of missing data (Zhang, et al. 2024b).
Hyperparameter optimization is crucial for fine-tuning 
deep learning models to achieve optimal performance. Tech-
niques such as Bayesian Optimization, Genetic Algorithms, 
and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) are widely used 
for efficient hyperparameter tuning (Narayanan and Ganesh 
2024). However, this study introduces Particle Swarm Dan-
delion Optimization (PSDO), a novel hybrid algorithm that 
combines the global exploration capabilities of PSO with 
the local exploitation strengths of Dandelion Optimization. 
PSDO ensures efficient hyperparameter tuning, leading to 
improved model accuracy and reduced computational costs.
Feature extraction plays a fundamental role in identify-
ing relevant patterns in satellite images, essential for dis-
tinguishing water bodies from other land cover types. Deep 
learning-based techniques such as Inception modules, 
Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks, and Multiscale Convo-
lutional Modules have proven effective in this domain (Gu 
and Zeng 2024). The proposed Multiscale Strip Convolution 
Module (MSSCM) captures spatial and spectral informa-
tion across multiple scales, enabling the model to adapt to 
the diverse appearances of water bodies in satellite images 
(Deng, et al. 2024).

Related work
In recent years, the segmentation of water bodies from satel-
lite imagery has attracted significant attention, with numer-
ous approaches proposed to address the inherent challenges 
of noise, data gaps, and complex spectral characteristics. 
Techniques such as data augmentation, noise reduction, 
pixel imputation, feature extraction, and segmentation have 
been extensively studied, leading to notable advancements 
in improving the accuracy and reliability of water body 
analysis (Zhang, et al. 2024c). This section reviews the 
existing literature on these techniques and highlights their 
relevance to this study.
In the context of satellite image augmentation, Genera-
tive Adversarial Networks (GANs) and their variants have 
become popular tools for creating synthetic datasets. For 
example, Wang et al. utilized CycleGAN for augmenting 
satellite images with diverse environmental conditions, 
improving the robustness of segmentation models (Wang, 
et al. 2025). Additionally, StyleGAN2 was explored by Feng 
et al. for high-quality augmentation, achieving significant 
improvements in model generalization. However, issues such 
as mode collapse and lack of fine-grained details remain 
challenges, which StyleGAN3 aims to overcome (Feng, et al. 
2024a).
Noise reduction has been a critical area of research in 
satellite image processing due to sensor limitations and 
environmental interference. Convolutional Neural Networks 
(CNNs) like DnCNN have been widely adopted for denois-
ing, with proven success in preserving structural details in 
images (Karthikeyan et al. 2024a). Furthermore, Attention-
Guided Denoising Autoencoders, as proposed by Tang et al., 
have shown the ability to focus on important image regions 
while reducing noise, leading to enhanced segmentation 
accuracy. These advancements underscore the importance 
of integrating attention mechanisms for effective denoising 
(Tang, et al. 2024).
Pixel imputation techniques have evolved to address miss-
ing or corrupted data in satellite imagery. Deep learning 
models like PixelCNN have been applied for probabilistic 
imputation, demonstrating improved accuracy in restoring 
image integrity (Popovici 2025; Celik and Eltawil 2024). 
Moreover, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been 
explored for their temporal modeling capabilities. For 
instance, Bi-ConvRNN has been utilized by Lui et al. for 
imputation in multitemporal satellite datasets, effectively 
capturing both spatial and temporal dependencies (Liu, et al. 
2024a).
Hyperparameter optimization plays a crucial role in 
improving the performance of deep learning models for sat-
ellite image segmentation. Conventional approaches such as 
grid search and random search are computationally inten-
sive and often fail to efficiently navigate high-dimensional 
parameter spaces (Yasin and Kornel 2024). Recent advance-
ments have focused on bio-inspired algorithms, such as Par-
ticle Swarm Optimization (PSO), which balances explora-
tion and exploitation, and Dandelion Optimization (DO), 
known for its effective local search capabilities (Ezhilarasan, 
et al. 2024; Labato 2024). The integration of these tech-
niques into the Particle Swarm Dandelion Optimization 
(PSDO) algorithm has demonstrated significant advantages 
in achieving optimal hyperparameter configurations with 
reduced computational effort.

Feature extraction methods have also seen significant

Techniques such as Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks and 
Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) have been employed

Segmentation of water bodies has benefited immensely 
from the advancements in deep learning. Architectures 
like U-Net and DeepLabV3 + have been widely adopted 
for semantic segmentation tasks, achieving state-of-the-art 
results in delineating water bodies from complex satellite 
imagery (Ramos and Sappa 2025). For instance, Jonnala 
et al. utilized a U-Net variant with skip connections, signifi-
cantly enhancing segmentation performance in noisy data-
sets. The adoption of specialized architectures such as Map 
U-Net has further demonstrated improved precision in han-
dling mixed land–water boundaries (Jonnala, et al. 2025).
Transformer-based segmentation models have been intro-
duced as an alternative to CNN architectures, utilizing self-
attention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies 
and enhance global feature extraction. Swin-Unet, proposed 
by Xiao et al., employs a hierarchical Transformer structure 
to improve multi-scale representation, while TransUNet, 
developed by Rami et al., integrates a Transformer encoder 
within a U-Net framework, achieving notable segmenta-
tion accuracy across various domains (Xiao, et al. 2024). 
Despite these advantages, Transformer-based models were 
not included in this study due to their higher computational 
complexity and extensive data requirements. Unlike CNN-
based architectures, which are optimized for efficiency, 
Transformers impose greater memory costs and require 
large-scale labeled datasets, making them less practical 
for large-scale remote sensing applications. The proposed 
approach instead leverages MSSCM, which effectively cap-
tures multiscale spatial-spectral features while maintaining a 
lower computational footprint. Future research will explore 
hybrid CNN-Transformer architectures to evaluate their fea-
sibility for water body segmentation in remote sensing. The

Proposed methodology
This section outlines the proposed framework for the seg-
mentation of water bodies from satellite images, as illus-
trated in Fig. 1. The methodology comprises five main 
stages: dataset selection, data preprocessing, hyperparam-
eter optimization, feature extraction, and segmentation. 
Each stage integrates state-of-the-art techniques to address 
specific challenges in satellite image analysis. The frame-
work begins with the selection of high-resolution satellite 
imagery from Sentinel-2 datasets, followed by preprocess-
ing steps including data augmentation, noise reduction, and 
pixel imputation to improve the quality and diversity of 
the dataset. Next, hyperparameter optimization techniques 
ensure efficient parameter tuning for the subsequent stages. 
Advanced feature extraction methods are then applied to 
capture multiscale spatial features. Finally, the segmenta-
tion of water bodies is achieved using a specialized Map 
U-Net architecture, tailored for accurate delineation of water 
regions in complex landscapes.

satellite imagery, selected for its advanced capability in cap-

sive coverage of diverse water bodies, including lakes, riv-
ers, reservoirs, and coastal zones. Its high-frequency tem-
poral revisit capability ensures the availability of up-to-date 
imagery, making it an invaluable resource for dynamic and

Noise reduction using attention guided denoising 
autoencoder with skip connection (AG‑DAES)
The Attention Guided Denoising Autoencoder with Skip 
Connection (AG-DAES) is designed to remove noise from 
satellite imagery while preserving spatial and spectral integ-
rity. As shown in Fig. 4, AG-DAES employs a multi-encoder 
structure where spectral and spatial filtering isolate critical 
features before being processed by convolutional layers with 
different kernel sizes. An attention mechanism selectively 
enhances relevant features, while skip connections ensure 
the retention of fine details. The decoder reconstructs the 
denoised image using transposed convolutional layers, 
guided by a loss function combining mean squared error 
and structural similarity index to balance spectral and spatial 
accuracy. This architecture effectively addresses complex 
noise patterns in satellite imagery, arising from atmospheric 
disturbances and sensor limitations. Its adaptability to mul-
tiple resolutions ensures broad applicability across various 
datasets, enhancing the dataset's quality for tasks such as 
water body segmentation and classification.
Pixel imputation using Bidirectional Convolutional 
Recurrent Neural Network (Bi‑ConvRNN)
Pixel imputation in this framework is performed using a 
Bidirectional Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (Bi-
ConvRNN), which reconstructs missing or corrupted spectral 
data by leveraging spatial–temporal dependencies. The model 
comprises a multi-layer encoder-decoder structure with spa-
tial–temporal Long Short-Term Memory (ST-LSTM) units at 
its core. As illustrated in Fig. 5, the input data, consisting of 
denoised spectral bands (RGB, NIR, SWIR) and a binary mask

The results highlight the effectiveness of the proposed meth-
odology in achieving accurate water body segmentation

ing techniques, optimized configurations, and multiscale

validating its robustness and adaptability in diverse environ-
mental conditions. These findings establish the framework

Experimental setup
The experiments were conducted on a high-performance 
computing environment featuring an NVIDIA RTX 3090 
GPU (24 GB VRAM), 64 GB RAM, and an AMD Ryzen 
9 5950X processor, running Ubuntu 20.04 LTS. The Sen-
tinel-2 dataset was split into 70% training, 20% validation, 
and 10% testing, ensuring a balanced distribution of different 
geographical regions and environmental conditions. Data 
augmentation techniques were applied to the training set to 
enhance generalization, while the validation set was used 
for hyperparameter tuning. The Adam optimizer (β₁ = 0.9, 
β₂ = 0.999) was employed with a learning rate of 0.002, 
optimized using Particle Swarm Dandelion Optimization 
(PSDO). The model was trained for 100 epochs with a batch 
size of 16, using the binary cross-entropy loss function for 
segmentation tasks. These configurations were fine-tuned to 
balance computational efficiency and model accuracy.
The dataset captures a diverse range of water bodies dis-
tributed across tropical, temperate, arid, and polar regions, 
ensuring a comprehensive representation of different terrains 
and environmental conditions. The training and validation 
process incorporates this geographical diversity; however, 
the study does not implement explicit cross-validation across 
multiple terrains. Future investigations will adopt geographi-
cally stratified cross-validation, where training and testing 
occur on distinct terrain types, to further assess the robust-
ness and generalization capability of the proposed frame-
work in previously unseen environmental settings.

Conclusion
This study proposed a comprehensive framework for accu-
rate water body segmentation in satellite imagery, integrat-
ing advanced methodologies to enhance segmentation per-
formance. StyleGAN3 was employed for data augmentation, 
generating diverse and realistic samples to mitigate overfit-
ting, while AG-DAES effectively handled noise reduction, 
preserving critical spatial details. Bi-ConvRNN addressed 
missing or corrupted data, ensuring precise pixel imputa-
tion, while hyperparameter optimization using the PSDO 
algorithm significantly improved model efficiency. The 
MSSCM module further enhanced feature extraction by cap-
turing spatial and spectral characteristics at multiple scales. 
The final Map U-Net architecture, integrating these opti-
mized components, delivered state-of-the-art segmentation 
accuracy, progressively improving from 92% to over 99%, 
outperforming existing deep learning-based segmentation 
models. These findings highlight the importance of inte-
grating preprocessing, optimization, and feature extraction 
techniques to address challenges such as mixed boundaries, 
noisy data, and complex transitions, with implications for 
environmental monitoring, water resource management, and 
disaster mitigation.

Abstract: Precise water body segmentation in satellite imagery plays a vital role in environmental monitoring, water resource man- agement, and disaster prevention. This study introduces a high-performance segmentation framework leveraging Sentinel-2 imagery, integrating advanced methodologies to enhance data integrity and segmentation accuracy. To increase dataset diversity and model generalization, StyleGAN3-based augmentation was implemented, yielding a 5% accuracy improvement over conventional methods. An Attention-Guided Denoising Autoencoder with Skip Connection (AG-DAES) was utilized for noise reduction, effectively preserving spatial details and strengthening segmentation robustness. To address missing and corrupted pixels, Bi-ConvRNN was employed for pixel restoration, significantly boosting performance. Additionally, the Particle Swarm Dandelion Optimization (PSDO) algorithm was used for hyperparameter tuning, contributing to an additional 3–5% accuracy gain. Feature extraction was refined through the Multiscale Strip Convolution Module (MSSCM), enhanc- ing spatial-spectral representation and leading to a 6–8% accuracy increase. The segmentation process was executed using the Map U-Net model, which, after integrating all proposed improvements, achieved state-of-the-art accuracy exceeding 99%. A comparative study demonstrated that the proposed framework outperforms existing methods, particularly in com- plex scenarios involving vegetation interference, occlusions, and mixed land–water transitions. This adaptable and scalable approach sets a new standard for water body segmentation in satellite image analysis, offering a powerful tool for future research in the field.
